newsitem.title: USA: Texas says Internet bill 'devastating' for gov'ts.
newsitem.headline: Texas says Internet bill 'devastating' for gov'ts.

text.p: An Internet taxation bill pending in the U.S. Congress would be "devastating" for state and local governments and bondholders, a Texas official warned a House panel Friday.
But industry representatives told the House telecommunications subcommittee that the Internet Tax Freedom Act is critically needed and represents prudent national policy.

"H.R. 1054 intrudes into state taxation in the most destructive manner possible," Wade Anderson, Texas comptroller of public accounts, told the panel at its first hearing on the bill sponsored by Rep. Christopher Cox, R-Calif.
Texas and its localities alone would lose $1.25 billion a year in property, sales and other taxes, Anderson told the panel, chaired by Rep. Billy Tauzin, R-La., a co-sponsor of the Cox bill.
Cox's bill and an identical measure introduced in the Senate by Ron Wyden, D-Ore., would impose an indefinite moratorium on state and local taxation of commerce over the Internet.

Committee action on Wyden's bill was postponed last month after states and localities raised concerns. Wyden subsequently agreed to "tighten" the bill's language to make clear that it covers only Internet-specific taxes, not sales, income, property taxes involving computer technology.

Michael Liddick, director of taxes at America Online, Inc., the largest Internet provider, lauded the Internet bills. He said a growing web of "inconsistent and difficult to comprehend" state and local taxes could strangle the company financially.
"Compliance with hundreds, if not thousands, of individual tax collection requirements would place a significant financial burden on the campany," Liddick said.

Mark Rhoads, legislative director for the U.S. Internet Council, said the bill would head off a "premature proliferation of patchwork Internet-specific taxes" by thousands of local governments. The council is a consortium of major corporations and public groups like the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.
Tauzin warned that some localities see the Internet as "the next pot of revenue to fill their shrinking budgets." Instead, they should view it as a "tax-free zone," he said.

"The revenue generated from growing Internet activity within a State or locality -- in terms of jobs, services and products -- will more than offset the small losses in direct Internet tax revenue," Tauzin said.
Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers told a congressional panel in April that the Administration strongly backs the "goals and underlying objectives" of the House and Senate bills.

The bills call for a national moratorium on taxes that specifically target the Internet, such as taxes on Internet access or online services. They also call for a two-year study of U.S. and foreign taxation of Internet commerce.
